lesson.title: Different Rules for Different Zones: Piecewise Functions
lesson.summary: A piecewise function stitches together separate formulas, each ruling over its own slice of the domain, into a single function.
lesson.body:
A piecewise function is a single function that is defined by two or more different formulas, each one applying only to a specific part of the domain. Instead of one equation controlling the entire graph the way y = 2x + 1 does, a piecewise function switches from rule to rule as x crosses certain boundary values, the way a phone plan might charge one rate for the first few gigabytes of data and a different rate after that.

Piecewise functions are written with a brace that lists each formula next to the interval of x-values where it applies, and those intervals must not overlap: every allowed input has to fall into exactly one piece, never two, or the vertical line test would fail and the whole thing would stop being a function. As long as the pieces divide the domain cleanly, the result is still one function, just built out of several formulas working in sequence.

Consider a shipping company that charges a flat 5 dollars for any package weighing up to and including 2 pounds, and then adds 2 dollars for every pound over that. Written as a piecewise function of weight w, C(w) = 5 for 0 < w <= 2, and C(w) = 5 + 2(w - 2) for w > 2. To find the cost of a 5-pound package, use the second piece because 5 is greater than 2: C(5) = 5 + 2(5 - 2) = 5 + 2(3) = 5 + 6 = 11 dollars.

Boundary values deserve extra care in a piecewise function. At exactly w = 2, the definition says to use the first rule, so C(2) = 5. Checking what the second rule would have predicted just above 2, as w approaches 2, gives C(w) = 5 + 2(w - 2), which approaches 5 + 2(0) = 5 as well. The two pieces meet up perfectly at w = 2, so this particular piecewise function happens to be continuous even though it is built from separate rules, while other piecewise functions, like the vending-machine or shipping-bracket examples in nearby chapters, jump abruptly at their boundaries instead.

Not every piecewise function connects smoothly at its boundaries the way the shipping example does. A cell phone plan that costs 20 dollars flat for up to 3 GB of data, then jumps to a 45 dollar premium tier the instant a customer crosses 3 GB, would be written as P(g) = 20 for 0 < g <= 3 and P(g) = 45 for g > 3. At g = 3 the cost is 20, but the instant g exceeds 3, even by a small fraction of a gigabyte, the cost leaps to 45, a jump of 25 dollars with no values in between. That kind of piecewise function is not continuous, and it previews the step functions covered next, which are built entirely from jumps like this one.

You have actually already met a piecewise function without the label: the absolute value function, f(x) = |x|, is defined as x when x is greater than or equal to 0, and as -x when x is less than 0, two separate linear rules stitched together at x = 0. Recognizing that connection now will make the step functions and absolute value graphs in the next chapters feel like natural extensions of the idea rather than new tricks.
